nodes.label: Outline of the rules of contract law: agreement, consideration, intention, terms, vitiating factors, discharge, remedies
Theory of contract law: freedom of contract vs consumer protection, classical vs modern approaches, bargain theory
Offer: a definite promise to be bound on specific terms (Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co)
Invitation to treat distinguished from an offer (Fisher v Bell, Pharmaceutical Society of GB v Boots, Gibson v Manchester CC)
Acceptance: unconditional agreement to all terms of the offer
Communication of acceptance must generally reach the offeror (Entores v Miles Far East)
Postal rule: acceptance effective on posting (Adams v Lindsell)
Revocation of offer: must be communicated before acceptance (Byrne v Van Tienhoven, Routledge v Grant)
Revocation via a reliable third party is valid (Dickinson v Dodds)
Counter-offer destroys the original offer (Hyde v Wrench)
Intention to create legal relations: requirement that parties intend the agreement to be legally binding
Domestic and social agreements: rebuttable presumption of no intention to create legal relations (Balfour v Balfour, Jones v Padavatton)
Rebutting the domestic presumption where parties separated or relied to their detriment (Merritt v Merritt)
Commercial agreements: rebuttable presumption that intention to create legal relations exists (Edwards v Skyways)
Rebutting the commercial presumption by express words such as 'binding in honour only' (Rose & Frank v Crompton)
Consideration: something of value passing between the parties, the price of the promise (Currie v Misa)
Consideration need not be adequate: courts do not assess whether the bargain is a fair economic exchange (Chappell v Nestle)
Consideration must be sufficient: it must have some recognisable value in law (Thomas v Thomas)
Past consideration is not valid consideration (Re McArdle), with exception where act done at the promisor's request (Lampleigh v Braithwait, Pao On v Lau Yiu Long)
Performance of an existing public duty is not good consideration unless something extra is provided (Collins v Godefroy, Glasbrook Bros v Glamorgan CC)
Performance of an existing contractual duty owed to the same party is not good consideration unless a practical benefit is conferred (Stilk v Myrick; Williams v Roffey Bros)
Performance of an existing contractual duty owed to a third party can be good consideration (Scotson v Pegg, Pao On v Lau Yiu Long)
Doctrine of privity: only parties to a contract can sue or be sued on it (Tweddle v Atkinson, Dunlop v Selfridge)
Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999: a third party may enforce a term if the contract expressly allows it, or purports to confer a benefit on them (s.1)
Common law exceptions to privity: agency, assignment, and collateral contracts (Shanklin Pier v Detel Products)
Express terms: terms actually stated by the parties, orally or in writing
Terms implied in fact: the officious bystander and business efficacy tests (The Moorcock, Shirlaw v Southern Foundries)
Terms implied by law and by custom, including through prior dealing and trade custom
Consumer Rights Act 2015: statutory implied terms in consumer contracts - satisfactory quality, fitness for purpose, and description (ss.9-11)
Consumer Rights Act 2015: implied term that services be performed with reasonable care and skill (s.49)
Conditions: major terms going to the root of the contract, breach entitles termination and damages (Poussard v Spiers)
Warranties: minor terms, breach entitles damages only, not termination (Bettini v Gye)
Innominate terms: classification depends on the seriousness of the consequences of breach (Hong Kong Fir Shipping v Kawasaki Kisen Kaisha)

Exclusion/limitation clauses: incorporation requirements - signature, notice before/at contract formation, and course of dealing (L'Estrange v Graucob, Olley v Marlborough Court, Thornton v Shoe Lane Parking)
Exclusion/limitation clauses: contra proferentem rule - ambiguous clauses construed against the party relying on them
Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977: controls on exclusion clauses in business contracts - negligence liability for death/injury void (s.2(1)), other exclusions subject to reasonableness (s.2(2))
Consumer Rights Act 2015 Part 2: unfair terms in consumer contracts are not binding, including the fairness test and 'grey list' of potentially unfair terms
Misrepresentation: a false statement of fact made by one party which induces the other to enter the contract
Misrepresentation requires a statement of fact, not mere opinion (Bisset v Wilkinson) - though a false opinion by an expert can be actionable (Esso v Mardon)

Silence generally not misrepresentation, but half-truths and failure to correct a later-falsified statement are actionable (With v O'Flanagan); omission as misrepresentation in consumer contexts under the Consumer Protection from Unfair Trading Regulations 2008
Misrepresentation must induce the representee to enter the contract, i.e. actually relied upon (Edgington v Fitzmaurice, Attwood v Small)
Fraudulent misrepresentation: false statement made knowingly, without belief in its truth, or recklessly (Derry v Peek)
Negligent misrepresentation under s.2(1) Misrepresentation Act 1967: representor must prove reasonable grounds for belief
Innocent misrepresentation: false statement made with reasonable belief in its truth
Remedies for misrepresentation: rescission for all types, damages for fraudulent (tort of deceit) and negligent (s.2(1)), damages in lieu of rescission under s.2(2)
Economic duress: illegitimate pressure that vitiates consent to a contract or variation
Economic duress requires illegitimate pressure amounting to a threat, not mere hard bargaining (Pao On v Lau Yiu Long)
Economic duress requires the victim to have no practical/realistic alternative but to submit (The Atlantic Baron; Universe Tankships v ITWF)
Economic duress requires the illegitimate pressure to be a significant cause of entering the contract (B&S Contracts v Victor Green; DSND Subsea v Petroleum Geo-Services)
Remedy for economic duress: the contract is voidable, allowing rescission
Discharge by performance: general rule requires precise and complete performance of contractual obligations (Cutter v Powell)
Exception: severable/divisible obligations allow partial payment for partial performance
Exception: doctrine of substantial performance allows payment less a deduction for defects (Hoenig v Isaacs)
Exception: where the innocent party is prevented from completing performance by the other party, a quantum meruit claim may arise (Planche v Colburn)
Exception: acceptance of partial performance by the other party requires payment for what was accepted (Sumpter v Hedges)
Frustration: a contract is discharged where, after formation, an unforeseen event makes performance impossible, illegal, or radically different from that contemplated (Taylor v Caldwell)
Frustrating event: physical impossibility, e.g. destruction of subject matter or unavailability of a party (Taylor v Caldwell)
Frustrating event: supervening illegality, e.g. outbreak of war (Fibrosa v Fairbairn)
Frustrating event: radical change of circumstances defeating the commercial purpose (Krell v Henry, contrasted with Herne Bay Steam Boat v Hutton)

Limits on frustration: self-induced frustration is not permitted (Maritime National Fish v Ocean Trawlers), and mere increased expense/hardship does not frustrate a contract (Davis Contractors v Fareham UDC)
Effect of frustration: contract automatically discharged for the future; financial adjustment under the Law Reform (Frustrated Contracts) Act 1943
Actual breach: failure to perform an obligation when performance is due

Anticipatory breach: a party indicates before performance is due that they will not perform (Hochster v De La Tour), giving the innocent party the option to accept the breach immediately or wait for performance (White & Carter v McGregor)
Consequences of breach depend on the type of term broken: repudiatory breach of a condition allows termination plus damages, breach of warranty allows damages only
Compensatory damages: aim to put the innocent party in the position they would have been in had the contract been performed (expectation loss), or the position before the contract (reliance loss)
Causation in damages: the breach must be an effective/factual cause of the claimant's loss

Remoteness of damage: recoverable losses limited to those arising naturally from the breach, or reasonably within the contemplation of both parties at the time of contracting (Hadley v Baxendale, applied in Victoria Laundry v Newman Industries)

Mitigation of loss: the claimant must take reasonable steps to minimise their loss and cannot recover for losses that reasonable mitigation would have avoided (British Westinghouse v Underground Electric Railways)
Specific performance: equitable order compelling a party to perform their contractual obligations, granted at the court's discretion typically where damages are inadequate (e.g. unique goods/land)
Injunction: equitable order restraining a party from breaching a negative contractual obligation, granted at the court's discretion
Equitable remedies are discretionary and subject to equitable maxims (e.g. must come with clean hands, no undue delay, not available where damages are adequate)
Consumer Rights Act 2015 remedies for goods: short-term right to reject, right to repair or replacement, and right to a price reduction or final right to reject (ss.20-24)
Consumer Rights Act 2015 remedies for services: right to repeat performance or a price reduction where service not performed with reasonable care and skill (ss.54-56)
Evaluation: offer and acceptance rules provide certainty but the postal rule can produce unfair results where letters are lost or delayed
Evaluation: the offer/invitation to treat distinction gives flexibility in commercial negotiation but can be technical and produce arbitrary outcomes (e.g. shop displays)

Evaluation: presumptions on intention to create legal relations can be criticised as based on outdated assumptions about domestic relationships (Balfour v Balfour) and create uncertainty at the margins
Evaluation: not requiring adequacy of consideration upholds freedom of contract and party autonomy
Evaluation: not requiring adequacy of consideration can permit unfair or exploitative bargains to stand
Evaluation: the practical benefit test in Williams v Roffey Bros creates inconsistency and arguably undermines the certainty of Stilk v Myrick
Evaluation: the past consideration rule can produce harsh outcomes where a genuine later promise to pay for an earlier act is unenforceable, mitigated somewhat by the Lampleigh v Braithwait exception
Evaluation: the strict privity doctrine caused injustice to intended beneficiaries who could not enforce contracts made for their benefit (Tweddle v Atkinson)
Evaluation: the Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999 successfully allows third parties to enforce benefits while respecting the original parties' intentions
Evaluation: the 1999 Act is limited because it requires the contract to expressly identify the third party or class, and parties can exclude its operation entirely
Evaluation: implied terms fill gaps and give effect to the presumed intentions of the parties, but the business efficacy/officious bystander tests are subjective and unpredictable
Evaluation: the Consumer Rights Act 2015 significantly strengthens consumer protection by consolidating and clarifying statutory implied terms and remedies
Evaluation: the innominate term approach (Hong Kong Fir) offers flexibility and fairness but creates uncertainty for parties as to their rights, since classification is only known after breach

Evaluation: the rigid condition/warranty classification offers certainty of remedy in advance but can produce disproportionate outcomes (e.g. termination for a trivial breach of a labelled 'condition')
Evaluation: UCTA 1977 and the Consumer Rights Act 2015 provide important protection against unfair exclusion clauses, but the reasonableness/fairness tests still create uncertainty in application

Reform proposals for contract formation and terms: e.g. codification of contract law, clearer statutory rules on communication of acceptance in electronic contracting, reform of consideration doctrine
